Using data collected by the LHCb experiment at the Large Hadron Collider, totaling 3.0 inverse femtobarns, the decay rate width difference for $B^0_s$ mesons into a $K^+K^-$ pair has been calculated. This calculation was made possible by identifying a specific decay channel and measuring the time it takes for the $B^0_s$ mesons to decay. The calculation yielded a value of $0.081$ plus or minus $0.025$ (statistical uncertainty) or $0.020$ (systematic uncertainty) inverse picoseconds, which is in agreement with theoretical predictions.

This research paper focuses on the numerical analysis of a discrete control problem associated with a random stochastic equation. The equation in question is influenced by a fractional derivative of a specific type, a singular time delay, and both a source term and boundary conditions that exhibit varying degrees of irregularity. The study involves the development and examination of numerical methods, including finite element techniques for spatial discretization and a spectral method for handling the fractional component of the equation in time. The paper establishes the convergence rates for the proposed numerical scheme, which are found to be 2 for the regular case and 1 for the irregular case, in terms of the solution's accuracy.

The Pierre Auger Observatory has detected the most energetic cosmic rays, with energies exceeding 4 EeV, and found that their arrival directions are not uniformly distributed across the sky. Researchers have analyzed the anisotropies in the arrival directions of these high-energy cosmic rays, finding that at energies between 4 and 14 EeV, the most energetic events are concentrated in the direction of the Large Magellanic Cloud. However, at energies above 14 EeV, the anisotropies become more complex, with the Small Magellanic Cloud appearing in the data. The anisotropies observed in the data are consistent with simulations of the effects of the Magellanic Clouds on the distribution of high-energy cosmic rays.

The study investigates the behavior of flow in lead-lead collisions at the LHC, specifically focusing on the variation of centrality and impact parameter. The analysis of the data reveals that the centrality-dependent behavior of the longitudinal flow coefficient, $\beta_{1}$, can be explained by a hydrodynamic model. The model successfully describes the observed trends in the data, including the variation of the elliptic flow coefficient, $v_{2}$, and the mean transverse momentum, $\langle p_{T} \rangle$, with respect to centrality. The study also examines the correlation between the elliptic flow and the longitudinal flow, finding that the ratio of the coefficients, $v_{2}/\beta_{1}$, remains constant across different centralities. The results are consistent with the predictions of the hydrodynamic model, which takes into account the initial geometry of the collision and the evolution of the quark-gluon plasma.

This research focuses on resolving inconsistencies in tables that contain empty cells and functional dependencies. It defines a new type of inconsistency called a "gap" and proposes a method to manage these discrepancies using a revised version of the standard repair process. The paper also presents an algorithm to find the most efficient way to fix these discrepancies and demonstrates its effectiveness through various examples.

This paper introduces a novel statistical model called the temporal varying Poisson autoregressive (TVPAR) model, which is designed to forecast future values in time series data based on past values. The TVPAR model is an extension of the Poisson autoregressive (PAR) model, which incorporates time-varying parameters that are influenced by previous values in the series. The paper presents the theoretical foundations of the TVPAR model, as well as a maximum likelihood estimation method for determining the model's parameters. The paper also includes a Monte Carlo simulation study to evaluate the performance of the estimation method, as well as an analysis of real-world data to demonstrate the practical application of the TVPAR model.

The integration of 3D object representations into robotic manipulation systems has been a significant area of research, with notable advancements made in recent years. However, existing object representations often fall short in capturing the spatial relationships between an object's features and its global coordinates. This limitation can hinder the effective utilization of these representations in various robotic tasks, such as object pose estimation and grasping. To address this issue, we introduce Neural Description Fields (NDF), a novel object representation that is inherently equivariant to rigid transformations. NDF utilizes a neural network to generate a compact, 3D-aware object description in the form of a feature vector. We demonstrate the effectiveness of NDF in two distinct robotic tasks, including pose estimation and grasp synthesis, and achieve superior performance compared to state-of-the-art methods.

Our calculations cover the three primary $O(N)$ universality classes: $O(0)$, $O(2)$, and $O(4)$, which are relevant to various physical phenomena, including the Ising universality class ($N=1$), the XY universality class ($N=2$), and the $SU(2)$ universality class ($N=4$). In this work, we establish the local convexity of the TAP free energy within the context of high-dimensional statistics, specifically for general symmetric random matrix ensembles. Our approach involves deriving a new inequality, which we term the Sudakov-Fernique post-AMP inequality, building upon the iterative message passing framework introduced by Benaych-Georges, Kabani, and Najim. This new inequality enables us to demonstrate the local convexity of the TAP free energy, as well as provide novel, independent proofs of previously established results by Benaych-Georges and Kabani for Gaussian and spiked covariance matrix ensembles.

Astronomical photometry can be used to measure the density of aerosols in the atmosphere, which is important for understanding their impact on climate and health. By analyzing the light from stars, astronomers can determine the amount of aerosols present in the air and how they affect the transmission of light over long distances. This research focuses on the theoretical framework for using photometry to measure aerosols, as well as the practical applications of this method in various fields, including astronomy, meteorology, and remote sensing. The paper also discusses the limitations of using photometry to measure aerosols and the challenges that need to be addressed to improve the accuracy of these measurements. Overall, this research highlights the potential of using astronomical photometry to better understand the complex interactions between the atmosphere and the Earth's surface.

This paper presents a novel approach to pose estimation that integrates two key components: a clustering module to predict 2D joint locations and a correspondence learning module to match joints with their 3D counterparts. By combining these modules, our method overcomes the limitations of existing techniques, which often rely on either clustering or correspondence learning alone. Our approach is designed to handle complex 3D objects and can be applied to both 2D images and point clouds. We have developed a new loss function to optimize the correspondence learning module, which incorporates a correspondence-aware attention mechanism. Our method is trained end-to-end and achieves state-of-the-art results on multiple datasets, including ShapeNet, S3DIS, and SHREC 2019. Our code is available at https://github.com/chenyuheng/DeepHMap++.

High-dimensional data analysis is crucial in fields like finance, biology, and social sciences. A key challenge in this area is accurately representing the complex relationships between variables. Graphical models, specifically conditional independence graphs, provide a powerful framework for this task. However, inferring these models from data can be computationally demanding, especially when dealing with non-Gaussian data. The Generalized Graphical Lasso method is a popular approach for this purpose, but existing implementations have limitations in terms of efficiency and flexibility. We present GGLasso, a Python library that overcomes these limitations by implementing a highly efficient algorithm for Generalized Graphical Lasso calculation. GGLasso is built on top of SciPy and NetworkX, and includes a user-friendly interface for data input and model inference. Our library also provides a variety of data visualization tools to aid in the interpretation of results. We demonstrate the effectiveness of GGLasso through a case study involving the analysis of gene expression data.

The configurational space of complex molecular systems is often characterized by high dimensionality and rugged landscapes, which pose significant challenges for efficient and accurate sampling of their properties. Molecular dynamics simulations are commonly used to sample these properties, but their computational cost can be prohibitive for large-scale systems. We present a novel approach to address this issue by introducing a stochastic differential equation that incorporates a time-dependent metric tensor, which can be used to modify the computational cost of simulations while maintaining their accuracy. Our approach is validated through extensive testing on a range of molecular systems, including the folding of a complex protein, the formation of a membrane, and the behavior of a polymer melt. Our results demonstrate that our approach can significantly reduce the computational cost of simulations while maintaining their accuracy, making it a valuable tool for the study of complex molecular systems.

The concept of prominence in eigenvectors has been a valuable tool for analyzing single-layer networks, aiding in the identification of community structures and the detection of anomalous data. However, its application to multilayer networks is still in its early stages. In this study, we introduce a novel approach to defining prominence in multilayer networks by considering the importance of nodes across different network layers. This new definition is based on the sum of the absolute values of the components of the eigenvector, and it is shown to possess desirable mathematical properties. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our definition is consistent with the existing definition of prominence in single-layer networks. We also provide a method for calculating the new definition of prominence and apply it to both single-layer and multilayer networks to showcase its effectiveness.

In this paper, we derive Dirac's formula for the squared Laplacian operator in R-Minkowski spacetimes, which are defined by the metric $ds^2 = \sum_{i=1}^n dx_i^2 - \sum_{j=1}^m dx_{n+j}^2$. Our derivation utilizes the properties of the Dirac operator in this specific spacetime context.

The liquid entry surface tension (LIST) phenomenon, which occurs when a solid object enters a liquid, has been extensively studied for flat surfaces. However, the dynamics of curved objects entering liquids remain relatively unexplored. This research investigates the LIST phenomenon for spheres entering liquids at varying speeds, with the aim of understanding the underlying mechanisms. The study found that the behavior of spheres can be categorized into three distinct regimes based on the entry speed: a low-speed regime where the sphere becomes fully submerged, a medium-speed regime where the air trapped inside forms a thin film, and a high-speed regime where the sphere remains partially submerged. The study also examined the effects of fluid viscosity and surface tension on the behavior of spheres, as well as the impact of the sphere's surface roughness on the formation of air films. The findings of this research provide valuable insights into the LIST phenomenon for curved objects and have potential applications in various fields, including fluid dynamics, engineering, and physics.

We investigate the generic structure of the low-energy effective field theory for Type IIB string theory, incorporating all possible operators up to a specific mass scale, and incorporating the effects of fluxes, branes, and moduli stabilization. We categorize the generic operators based on their symmetry-breaking properties and find that certain operators, which are not protected by any symmetries, are expected to be present and have a significant impact on the theory. We find that these operators, which are not suppressed by any powers of the string coupling constant, can be classified into two categories: those that break the shift symmetry of the axio-dilaton and those that break the shift symmetry of the Kähler moduli. We also find that these operators can be classified based on their scaling behavior with respect to the string coupling constant and the Planck mass, and that they can be grouped into two categories: those that are not suppressed by any powers of the string coupling constant and those that are suppressed by powers of the string coupling constant. We find that these operators can have a significant impact on the theory, and that they can be used to construct a generic model of moduli stabilization that is consistent with the observed properties of the universe.

Cubanite, a common sulfide mineral, is known for its distinctive copper luster and is frequently mistaken for chalcopyrite. Recent studies have shown that cubanite is a Mott insulator, and its electronic properties are influenced by the presence of iron and copper. This study investigates the electronic structure of cubanite using density functional theory and dynamical mean-field theory, and finds that the material exhibits orbital-selective behavior, where the iron 3d orbitals are localized and the copper 3d orbitals are itinerant. The study also explores the impact of structural distortions on the material's electronic properties and finds that the presence of disorder can lead to the formation of impurity bands and the suppression of orbital-selective behavior. Overall, this study provides new insights into the complex electronic properties of cubanite and highlights the importance of considering orbital degrees of freedom in the study of transition metal sulfides.

We experimentally observed massive exciton Rabi oscillations in a GaAs/AlGaAs quantum well structure without an external magnetic field. By applying an alternating laser field, we modulated the density of dark excitons and measured their absorption, revealing Rabi oscillations in the dark exciton population. The oscillation frequency was found to be proportional to the alternating laser field strength, and we estimated the effective Rabi frequency to be approximately 1.5 MHz per 100 W/cm^2. Our findings demonstrate that dark excitons can be effectively manipulated using alternating laser fields, which is crucial for developing quantum information processing technologies based on dark excitons.

Lattice structures are highly effective in creating functional materials, yet their symmetrical properties can lead to the misplacement of Dirac points. This issue can be overcome by utilizing non-symmorphic lattice types, which are capable of accurately positioning Dirac points. This study focuses on a two-dimensional wallpaper category lattice, specifically the p2mg type, and investigates the electronic properties of a model Hamiltonian. By analyzing the Hamiltonian, we demonstrate that Dirac points can be precisely located at high symmetry points in the Brillouin zone, and their positions can be manipulated through the introduction of a mass term. Furthermore, we explore the effects of various lattice parameters on the band structure and surface states, and also examine the impact of spin-orbit coupling and lattice distortions on the system.

Quantum-optical catalysis is a process that involves the interaction of a single photon with a quantum system, resulting in the production of a coherent state. This process is of great interest in the field of quantum information processing, as it can be used to generate non-classical states that are essential for various quantum protocols. In this paper, we investigate the properties of single-photon facilitated coherent states (SFCS) and their potential applications in quantum information processing. We derive the expression for the average photon number and the Wigner function of the SFCS, and we also examine their behavior under different conditions. We find that the average photon number of the SFCS is lower than that of a coherent state with the same amplitude, and that the Wigner function of the SFCS exhibits a characteristic pattern that is indicative of its non-classical nature. We also examine the entanglement properties of the SFCS, and we find that they can be used to generate a wide range of non-Gaussian states that are essential for various quantum protocols. In summary, this paper provides a detailed analysis of the properties of single-photon facilitated coherent states and their potential applications in quantum information processing.

The application of the Newman-Penrose formalism to the Einstein field equations is a powerful tool in general relativity. This approach involves the use of a complex null tetrad, which can be derived from a real null tetrad. In this paper, we demonstrate how to construct a real null tetrad from the electromagnetic field bivector in the context of the Newman-Penrose framework. We also explore the possibility of deriving a real null tetrad from the Weyl curvature bivector.

This paper presents a novel approach to generating polymers using a combination of linear regression and whole programming. The proposed method involves creating a mathematical model that can be used to generate new polymers that are similar to a given set of input data. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through the generation of new chemical compounds that are similar to a set of input data. The results show that this approach can be used to generate new polymers that are similar to a given set of input data.

Accurate segmentation of esophageal tumors is a critical step in the treatment planning process for these neoplasms. However, the task is complicated by the fact that the esophagus is a narrow, tubular structure that is often difficult to visualize in CT scans due to its low contrast and frequent presence of folds and luminal contents. In this study, we present a novel deep learning-based segmentation method called the Esophageal Neoplasm Segmentation using the DDUnet. This method is based on a modified version of the Unet architecture that incorporates two key components: a dense block that enhances feature extraction and a focus attention module that helps the network prioritize the most relevant parts of the image. Our approach was evaluated on a dataset of 100 CT scans, and the results showed that our network achieved a Dice Similarity Coefficient of 0.81, which is a significant improvement over the original Unet architecture. Our code is available at the following URL: https://github.com/ahmedmohamed1999/Esophageal-Neoplasm-Segmentation-using-CT-Scans.

The rise of the internet and social media has led to a surge in multilingual communication, resulting in the development of code-switched speech and text. This phenomenon, where two or more languages are combined, is prevalent in many multilingual communities and poses challenges for natural language processing (NLP) tasks. The purpose of this paper is to provide a comprehensive overview of the existing NLP tasks that have been conducted in code-switched contexts, along with the obstacles and factors that influence the success of these tasks. The paper also includes a list of code-switched datasets and discusses the impact of various factors, such as the order of words, the presence of punctuation, and the use of diacritics, on NLP tasks. The findings of this research are expected to be beneficial for future NLP studies in multilingual contexts.

The rapid development of AI technology has led to the creation of various image captioning systems, which generate descriptions of visual content. However, the quality of these descriptions is difficult to assess due to the lack of human-generated reference information. To address this issue, researchers have developed methods for evaluating image captions based on the content of the images alone. Nevertheless, these methods do not take into account the context in which the captions are used. In this paper, we investigate the potential of using human-generated reference information to evaluate image captions. We found that this information can be effectively utilized to improve the quality of the assessment, particularly when the reference information is presented in a concise format. Additionally, we found that the assessment of captions based on human-generated reference information is more closely related to human judgments than assessments based on the content of the images alone.

Ta$_2$O$_5$ is a technologically important material with a complex crystal structure, making it a subject of interest for various applications. The material's properties are highly influenced by its crystal structure, which can be altered by external factors such as pressure and temperature. In this study, we investigate the base state crystal configuration of Ta$_2$O$_5$ by examining its structural, electronic, and thermodynamic properties. We used density functional theory to analyze the material's properties and found that its structure consists of two distinct layers of Ta atoms separated by an oxygen layer. We also found that the material exhibits metallic behavior and a high electron-phonon coupling constant, which may contribute to its superconducting properties. In addition, we employed Monte Carlo simulations to study the material's phase transitions and found that it exhibits a first-order transition from a low-temperature monoclinic phase to a high-temperature cubic phase. Our findings provide valuable insights into the complex crystal structure of Ta$_2$O$_5$ and its potential for various technological applications.

This study investigates the role of Big Geographic Arrangements (BGAs) in the spread of misinformation within Reddit communities in the United States. By examining the influence of various geographic factors, including time zones, states, and metropolitan areas, on the sharing of fake news, we found that time zones have a significant impact on the propagation of misinformation, whereas states and metropolitan areas do not. Furthermore, we discovered that the effect of time zones on the spread of misinformation is mediated by the user's engagement with Reddit, particularly through upvoting and commenting. The findings of this research have important implications for understanding the role of geography in the spread of misinformation and can inform the development of more effective strategies for combating misinformation online.

This research focuses on the spoken language patterns used by human instructors when guiding robots through complex tasks. Specifically, we investigate the types of speech that accompany hand gestures during these demonstrations. Our study involves analyzing the speech of instructors guiding robots through a task that requires manipulating an object with their hands. Our findings reveal that instructors' speech is characterized by a combination of specific features, including the use of grammatical structures, the presence of filler words, and the absence of certain sounds. These findings have implications for the development of more effective speech recognition systems and the creation of more natural-sounding robotic assistants.

This research paper explores the geometric intricacy of field theory by examining the Euler-Arnold equations, which describe the dynamics of a one-dimensional object. The study of these equations reveals that the underlying geometry is that of an infinite-dimensional space, specifically the group of diffeomorphisms of a circle. The authors demonstrate that the solutions to these equations can be visualized as geodesics on this geometric space, and that the geodesic curvature of these solutions can be used to quantify the complexity of the field theory. This connection between the geometric intricacy and the dynamics of the object is further explored through the use of variational principles and the study of conserved quantities. The results of this research provide a new perspective on the relationship between geometry and field theory, and may have implications for the development of more accurate models of physical systems.

Conversational systems are increasingly being used in various applications, from customer service to personal assistants. However, the lack of standardized evaluation methods has hindered the development of these systems. This paper proposes an automated evaluation framework that can be used to assess conversational bots. The framework is based on a set of evaluation metrics that measure the bot's ability to understand and respond to user input. The framework is implemented in Python and can be used to evaluate bots in a variety of settings. The paper also discusses the limitations of the framework and potential areas for future research.

With the rapid growth of e-commerce platforms, users are increasingly exposed to a vast array of products, making it difficult to make purchasing decisions. To address this challenge, personalized recommendation systems have become essential. However, traditional recommendation models often overlook the fact that products can be categorized by multiple aspects, such as brand, style, and function, which can significantly impact user preferences. To capture these complex preferences, we propose a novel multi-sparse-domain recommendation model called MSTCRL. This model incorporates a multi-aspect preference representation that captures user preferences across different product aspects, and employs a cooperative recommendation mechanism to share information across different sparse domains. MSTCRL leverages a contrastive learning framework to enhance the quality of shared information and improve the accuracy of recommendations. Experimental results on real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of MSTCRL in providing accurate recommendations.

This paper presents a solution to the conic formulation of the problem of maximizing the number of edges in a planar graph with $n$ vertices and $m$ edges, first introduced by D. S. Ramana in 2019. By utilizing a Julia package called Hypatia.jl, we were able to find a solution that satisfies the requirements of the formulation, which involves a second-order cone. The solution was achieved by determining the precise values of $n$, $m$, and a matrix $A$ that, when used to generate a graph, results in a planar graph with $n$ vertices and $m$ edges. The solution was found by starting with a known planar graph and adjusting its edges to increase the number of edges to $2n-4$. The final solution was verified using the Plantri program, which generates all possible planar graphs with a given number of vertices and edges.

The rapid advancement of MRI technology has led to a surge in research and clinical applications, but it has also resulted in a variety of MRI scanners with different specifications. This diversity has made it challenging to develop quality assurance (QA) protocols that are universally applicable. In this study, we investigate the underlying causes of the lack of generalization in deep learning-based QA protocols across different MRI scanners. Our findings reveal that the primary obstacle to generalization is the high dimensionality of the problem, which is compounded by the limited availability of training data. To address this issue, we propose a novel approach that leverages the inherent structure of MRI images to reduce the dimensionality of the problem. Our results demonstrate that this approach significantly improves the generalization capabilities of deep learning-based QA protocols across different MRI scanners.

The integration of private electric vehicles (EVs) into the power grid has been shown to significantly impact network resilience. However, the private nature of these vehicles complicates the coordination of their charging and discharging activities. This study proposes a novel approach to address this challenge by modeling private EVs as rational agents that seek to optimize their own interests. A multi-agent optimization framework is developed to balance the needs of the grid and the private EVs, with the goal of minimizing power losses and enhancing network resilience. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through simulations on a test feeder, with results indicating that the proposed method can effectively balance the needs of the grid and private EVs, while also improving network resilience.

This paper introduces a novel concept of multi-agent recurrent meetings, where autonomous agents repeatedly gather to exchange information and make decisions. Unlike existing research, our approach allows agents to make informed choices based on their past interactions and the outcomes of previous meetings. To achieve this, we developed a framework that enables agents to learn from their experiences and adjust their behavior accordingly. Our results demonstrate that this approach can lead to more efficient and effective decision-making in complex environments.

This paper presents a new approach to predicting the yields of rare baryons and mesons in high-energy proton-proton collisions. By utilizing a statistical model based on thermal equilibrium, we can forecast the production of rare particles, given the measured yields of common particles. The model's predictions are compared with experimental data from the LHC for various centralities and particle multiplicities. The results indicate that the model accurately predicts the production of rare particles in high-multiplicity events, but struggles to match the measured yields in low-multiplicity events. The discrepancy between the model's predictions and the measured data may be due to the influence of non-thermal processes on particle production.

A key result in combinatorial theory, known as the foundation theorem for Coxeter groups, establishes a connection between the Coxeter element of a Coxeter group and its associated graph. This theorem states that the sum of the lengths of the Coxeter element's conjugacy class equals twice the number of connected components of the graph that correspond to hyperbolic Coxeter components. However, this result is limited to Coxeter groups of the elliptic type. In this paper, we extend the proof of the foundation theorem to the B-type Coxeter groups.

Astronomical observations of distant supernovae and galaxies are influenced by gravitational lensing, which can be categorized into strong and weak effects. While strong lensing is easily identifiable, the more subtle weak lensing effect is more challenging to detect. This study aims to characterize the weak lensing impact on a large sample of 1024 Type Ia supernovae from the Pantheon dataset, which spans redshifts from 0.006 to 0.83. By analyzing the distribution of the lensing magnification, we found that the data aligns with theoretical predictions, albeit with some discrepancies at higher redshifts. Furthermore, we developed a method to estimate the matter distribution in the universe based on the observed weak lensing effects. This method yields an estimate of the matter density parameter, Omega_m, of 0.27, with an uncertainty of 0.07, which is consistent with other cosmological measurements.

This paper presents a novel design for a compact 3D photonic switch based on T-shaped hubs, which are critical components in ring resonator-based optical cross-connects. The proposed T-shaped hub design is optimized for a 1550nm wavelength and fabricated using silicon-on-insulator technology. The design features a 10dB crosstalk level, a 100nm free spectral range, and a 0.15nm insertion loss. The design's small footprint of 100x100 micrometers makes it highly suitable for integration into photonic circuits.

The integration of 3D point clouds into object detection systems has been a
significant advancement in recent years. However, the vast amount of data in
point clouds can be computationally expensive to process, particularly for
identifying objects that are not easily visible. This paper proposes a novel
method for determining the importance of context in 3D space, which can be
utilized by detection models to prioritize the processing of relevant data.
Our approach involves training a model to predict the 3D location of objects
based on their visual appearance, and then using this information to guide the
processing of detection models. Our method is evaluated on the KITTI dataset,
and the results demonstrate that our approach can significantly improve the
performance of detection models, particularly for objects that are not easily
visible.

This study investigates the existence of solutions for a Kirchhoff-type elliptic equation in $\mathbb{R}^3$, featuring a singular term and a nonlinear component that falls under the Trudinger-Moser category. By utilizing a penalization technique and variational methods, we establish the existence of solutions for this equation.

We investigate the sum of n independent and identically distributed random variables, each taking the form of -1 or 1, under a specific correlation constraint. This constraint is defined by the non-positive expected product of any two distinct variables. We establish that the probability of the sum's absolute value exceeding a certain threshold t is bounded by a function of t and n, specifically, a combination of exponential and polynomial terms. This bound is derived using a novel approach that combines Stein's method for distribution approximation with a method for bounding the variation in a random process. Our bound is shown to be comparable to existing results in the field, particularly those obtained through the logarithmic Sobolev inequality.

We introduce a new class of operations called symplectic modifications, which are defined as symplectic transformations that alter the canonical class of a manifold. These operations are analogous to topological surgeries and encompass various established techniques, including blow-ups, flops, and divisorial contractions. We demonstrate that symplectic modifications can be characterized as the most general class of symplectic transformations that maintain the manifold's symplectic nature while changing its canonical class. Additionally, we establish a fundamental property of these operations, stating that they are reversible.

In the context of kidney transplantation, a key factor influencing the success of a transplant is the compatibility between the donor and recipient. A critical aspect of this compatibility is the presence of preformed antibodies against donor antigens, measured by the Kidney Donor Antigen (KDA) score. While a low KDA score is generally favorable, a score of zero is considered ideal. This study investigates the prevalence of zero-KDA scores among kidney transplant candidates and examines the factors that contribute to this ideal state. The research reveals that zero-KDA scores are relatively rare, with a prevalence of 10% among patients awaiting a transplant and 17% among those who have received a transplant. The study also identifies several factors that increase the likelihood of a zero-KDA score, including a shorter waiting time, a lower risk of acute rejection, and a higher likelihood of receiving a living donor kidney. The findings suggest that patients with zero-KDA scores may have a higher chance of receiving a compatible kidney and experiencing better transplant outcomes.

This study investigates the semantic meaning of word representations in the context of financial sentiment analysis, specifically using the Loughran-McDonald financial dictionary. We employ the Word2Vec algorithm to generate word representations and apply the Procrustes distance metric to measure the semantic similarity between words with the same representation and those with opposite meanings. Our findings indicate that words with the same representation are semantically similar to their opposites, which is contrary to the expected behavior of a meaningful semantic space. Furthermore, we discovered that the Procrustes distance metric is not a reliable indicator of semantic similarity, as it is influenced by the magnitude of the word representations. Our results suggest that the Loughran-McDonald financial dictionary is not suitable for training sentiment analysis models that rely on the semantic meaning of word representations.

This paper presents the SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM variants of an integrated data and power transmission system, which utilizes broadband waveforms generated by multiple antennas and carriers. The analysis focuses on optimizing the system's performance in terms of data transmission efficiency and power transfer effectiveness. A key finding is that the system's performance can be significantly improved by adjusting the number of active antennas and carriers, with the optimal configuration depending on the system's specific requirements and constraints.

This research presents an embedded boundary method for solving a phase-field model that describes the transition between solid and liquid states. The approach uses a high-order spectral element method to discretize the spatial domain, with an interface between solid and liquid phases represented by an embedded boundary. A novel mixed level-set / embedded boundary technique is employed to accurately capture the interface, with the normal vector and curvature calculated to high order. A second-order accurate time-stepping scheme is used to discretize the time derivative in the governing equations. Numerical results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in capturing complex interface dynamics.

In the context of multiplayer games, we investigate the possibility of a learning process that results in rationalizable equilibria. We establish that this process is feasible for two-player games and demonstrate its impossibility for three-player games under specific conditions. Furthermore, we identify a class of three-player games where the learning process can indeed yield rationalizable equilibria.

The rapid spread of infectious diseases has led to the development of counterintuitive strategies, such as the "protective rewiring" hypothesis. This hypothesis suggests that infected individuals may disconnect from their existing social networks and form new connections with uninfected people, potentially slowing the epidemic's progression. To investigate this phenomenon, we created a mathematical model based on a dynamic network where infected individuals can sever existing connections and form new ones with uninfected individuals. Our analysis of this model reveals that the epidemic's progression is influenced by the rate at which connections are formed and broken, as well as the initial network's structure. Specifically, we found that the epidemic's progression can be characterized by three distinct phases: a period of rapid growth, a period of slow decline, and a period of rapid decline. Our findings provide valuable insights into the complex interplay between social networks and the spread of infectious diseases, and may inform the development of more effective public health interventions.

The concept of parton distribution functions (PDFs) is rooted in the 1960s, yet it remains a highly abstract and intricate subject.  PDFs are essentially probability densities that describe the likelihood of finding a parton within a hadron at a given momentum fraction, but their probabilistic nature is not straightforward to interpret.  This is due to the fact that individual partons are not observable, and their properties are influenced by quantum chromodynamics (QCD) and the renormalization scale.  As a result, PDFs are not truly probabilities, but rather a tool used to predict the outcomes of high-energy particle collisions.  This paper presents a theory framework that provides a more intuitive understanding of PDFs, and it is shown that PDFs can be viewed as a type of conditional expectation value, given certain conditions.  This framework also enables the calculation of the variance of PDFs, which is a measure of the uncertainty in the distribution of partons within a hadron.  This uncertainty is found to be significant, and it has important implications for the interpretation of PDFs and the prediction of particle collisions.

Reinforcement learning agents in complex environments often struggle due to limited data, which hinders their ability to learn effectively. To address this issue, researchers have developed experience replay techniques that allow agents to reuse past experiences. However, existing replay methods do not fully utilize the most valuable past experiences, which can limit the agent's performance. In this paper, we propose a novel replay method called Variance Decrease based Experience Replay (VDEXR) that prioritizes past experiences based on their variance, which is a measure of uncertainty. VDEXR is designed to reduce the uncertainty of the agent's policy by focusing on past experiences with high variance. We demonstrate the effectiveness of VDEXR in a range of simulated and real-world scenarios, including a simulated car-following task and a real-world car-following task. Our results show that VDEXR can significantly improve the performance of policy learning algorithms, especially in data-limited scenarios.

The rapid development of conversational agents has led to the creation of multi-turn dialogue datasets, which are essential for advancing research in this field. However, existing datasets are limited in terms of the diversity of dialogue structures they encompass. Most datasets primarily consist of linear dialogues, lacking the complexity found in real-world conversations that include phenomena such as interruptions, overlapping speech, and multiple conversational threads. To address this limitation, we have developed a novel multi-branching dialogue dataset called MultiTalk, which contains 10,000 multi-branching conversations with up to five conversational threads. We have also introduced a new task called multi-branching dialogue generation and proposed a baseline model for this task. Our experiments demonstrate that existing single-conversation generation models are not well-suited for this task, and we have identified several challenges and opportunities for future research in this field.

We have developed a new code, called cNbody, to efficiently simulate the evolution of dark matter in conformal linking gravity models. This code can handle various modified gravity theories, such as $f(R)$ gravity, by simulating the movement of $10^9$ particles in a cosmological volume within a few days on a high-performance computer. The cNbody code uses a second-order leapfrog algorithm to solve the equations of motion, and it can handle the complex interactions between particles and the gravitational field. We have also demonstrated that the cNbody code can accurately reproduce the results of previous simulations, and we have used it to explore the effects of modified gravity on the formation of galaxies.

We investigate the relationship between conformally invariant stochastic Loewner evolutions (CDSL) and the Gaussian free field (GFH) on a disk. Specifically, we examine the connection between the CDFH and the GFH on the domain, and we demonstrate that the boundaries of the CDFH clusters correspond to the boundaries of the CDFH clusters. Furthermore, we establish that the CDFH clusters are in one-to-one correspondence with the CDFH clusters.

MediaWiki, the underlying technology for Wikipedia, is a powerful tool for collaborative knowledge creation. However, its effectiveness is hindered by the fact that it is primarily used for finished products rather than works in progress. To address this limitation, we developed WorkingWiki, a customized MediaWiki-based platform designed to facilitate collaborative research projects. WorkingWiki offers a range of features, including customizable templates, user-specific dashboards, and integrated tools for managing tasks and discussions. We have successfully applied WorkingWiki to support a research project, demonstrating its potential as a versatile platform for collaborative work.

This research investigates the reaction of a turbulent jet fire to acoustic stimulation within a linearized framework. By utilizing an active flame technique, researchers can artificially induce oscillations in the flame, allowing for the examination of the flame's response to varying excitation amplitudes. The study focuses on a jet fire burning methane in an open environment, and the results are compared to linear stability theory predictions. The findings indicate that the flame's response to low-amplitude excitation is linear, but as the amplitude increases, the response becomes nonlinear, and the flame's oscillation frequency shifts. The study also highlights the importance of considering nonlinear effects when analyzing the stability of jet fires.

This essential tetrad field is required to define a nonlocal curvature tensor in a manner that is consistent with the principles of general covariance. The nonlocal action for this theory is derived, and the field equations are obtained by varying the action with respect to the essential tetrad field and the non-constitutive connection. A simplified version of the nonlocal gravitational theory is also considered, in which the connection is constitutive and determined by the essential tetrad field. The integration of functional genomic annotations with genome-wide association studies (GWAS) has been a subject of debate, with some studies suggesting that incorporating genomic annotations can enhance GWAS results, while others found no significant benefit. To investigate this issue further, we analyzed 18 human traits using a Bayesian framework, examining the association between GWAS data and the ENCODE functional genomic annotations. Our findings revealed that incorporating ENCODE annotations can improve GWAS results for 10 out of 18 traits, with notable improvements observed for traits such as height, weight, and blood pressure. However, the results were not uniform across all traits, with some showing no significant benefit from incorporating ENCODE annotations. Our study provides a comprehensive assessment of the utility of ENCODE annotations in improving GWAS results and highlights the need for a more nuanced understanding of the relationship between functional genomic information and GWAS results.

This paper provides an overview of the production mechanisms for single hadrons and mesons in proton-proton collisions at the LHC, focusing on rare occurrences of single hadrons or mesons. It delves into the production of individual hadrons and mesons, including pions, kaons, and protons, as well as exotic mesons like D-mesons and B-mesons. It also covers the production of heavy quarkonia, such as J/psi and Upsilon, and discusses the challenges and opportunities in studying tiny systems through tiny final states.

In the context of a polar molecule, we investigate the impact of linear electron-vibrational and spin-vibrational couplings that arise from the movement of the molecule's center of mass. We find that these couplings are proportional to the square of the vibrational frequency and the ratio of the molecule's size to the Bohr radius, resulting in extremely small coefficients. Consequently, these couplings are too weak to be significant in most scenarios.

The concept of semantic variety in discourse refers to the use of different words to convey the same meaning, a phenomenon that is crucial for effective communication. This study investigates the applicability of Natural Language Inference (NLI) models in predicting entailment relationships between semantically diverse texts. Our findings reveal that NLI models struggle to identify entailment when the hypothesis contains novel vocabulary not present in the premise. To address this challenge, we propose a novel task called the "New Word Entailment" (NWE) task, which involves training models on a dataset of 1,000 NWE pairs. Our results indicate that models trained on the NWE dataset can successfully predict entailment relationships between texts with new vocabulary, outperforming models trained on traditional NLI datasets.

This study uses numerical simulations to investigate the impact of rotation on brown dwarfs and giant planets, focusing on their internal structure, heat transfer, and observable characteristics. By modeling rotating objects with varying masses and rotation speeds, we found that rotation significantly affects the internal temperature distribution, leading to a more uniform temperature profile in rapidly spinning objects. This uniformity can be observed in infrared spectra, particularly in the shape of molecular absorption lines. Additionally, we found that rotation can alter the appearance of gravity-darkened objects, making them appear more like single-temperature objects with specific line broadening patterns. The study also found that rotation can delay the onset of convection in certain objects, leading to a more stable internal structure. Overall, this research provides valuable insights into the internal dynamics and observable characteristics of rotating brown dwarfs and giant planets.

This paper presents a Python-based Python package, pyimp, designed to facilitate the integration of experimental data into amplitude analyses. The tool enables the conversion of various file formats, including ROOT, into the IMP format, and can be utilized as a standalone program or as an importable module within amplitude assessment frameworks. The pyimp package is demonstrated through the analysis of the B^0_s -> J/\psi K^+K^- decay process.

A comprehensive analysis of 100 afterglows from gamma-ray bursts, spanning both short and long durations, was conducted using light curves and spectral data. By employing a generic model that incorporates the effects of magnetic fields and electron scattering, we were able to characterize the bursts' properties and their surrounding environments. The results revealed that the bursts can be divided into two groups based on their energy output: those with high and low energy. The distribution of environments around the bursts also showed a bimodal pattern, with most bursts occurring in environments with low densities and a smaller number in high-density environments. The relationship between the bursts' energy output and their surrounding environments was found to be consistent with theoretical predictions. The analysis also revealed that the bursts with high energy output and low-density environments were associated with the formation of neutron stars or black holes, while those with low energy output and high-density environments were associated with the formation of long-lived disks. The results of this study provide valuable insights into the nature of gamma-ray bursts and their surrounding environments.

Given a graph G and an integer k, the task of finding a way to split the vertices of G into two separate subgraphs G1 and G2, where the number of edges in G1 and G2 are both at most k, is known as the Bipartite Vertex Division problem. This paper presents an algorithm that can solve this problem efficiently, with a runtime of O(2.828^k + kp).

This paper presents a novel approach to bipedal locomotion that integrates active leg suspension, inspired by biological systems. By incorporating a linear actuator in each leg, our design offers significant advantages in terms of efficiency, obstacle negotiation, and terrain adaptability. We developed a control framework that leverages the actuator to recover from disturbances and maintain balance, enabling the robot to navigate challenging environments with greater agility. Our approach was tested on a custom-built bipedal robot, and the results demonstrate its ability to walk over various terrains, recover from unexpected disturbances, and even perform complex maneuvers like jumping and landing. Our findings suggest that active leg suspension can significantly enhance the capabilities of bipedal robots, opening up new possibilities for their use in a wide range of applications.

A field is considered respected when its multiplicative group can be divided into n subgroups, each with a distinct coset that forms a group isomorphic to the original. This concept is an extension of a previously defined property where the subgroups are not necessarily distinct. The paper provides a comprehensive list of respected fields with a specific property called a complete residue map, which is a function that maps the field to one of the respected subgroups. The authors also explore the relationship between respected fields and a related concept called a partitioned field, and provide a detailed examination of the properties of these fields.

The HyperDegrade framework is designed to dynamically adjust CPU performance in real-time based on application requirements and system conditions. By utilizing a feedback loop, HyperDegrade can efficiently manage CPU performance, reducing the need for constant monitoring and control. Experimental results show that HyperDegrade can achieve significant energy savings while maintaining acceptable application performance, outperforming traditional performance management techniques.

This paper presents a novel unknotting procedure for traditional and welded links, which are types of non-classical knots. The proposed method involves transforming the link into a virtual knot, applying unknotting moves to virtual crossings, and ultimately resolving the knot. The paper also includes an example of a welded knot that is unknotted using this procedure.

We demonstrate that the Vassiliev invariant of order three, denoted as $\nu_3$, when applied to the Fox-Hatcher loop $\mathrm{FH}_3$ in the three-torus $T^3$, yields a non-zero value. This finding is significant because it indicates that the Vassiliev invariant $\nu_3$ is not a trivial characteristic.

This paper presents a novel approach to multi-agent collaboration in a tactical setting, where agents are limited in their computational and communication capabilities. The proposed framework is designed to enable agents to work together effectively in a dynamic environment, where they must navigate and make decisions based on their individual observations. The framework is divided into two main components: a communication protocol that enables agents to exchange information in a structured manner, and a collaborative decision-making algorithm that allows agents to make joint decisions based on their individual observations. The framework is evaluated through a series of simulations, where it is shown to enable agents to work together effectively in a range of scenarios, including navigation and target acquisition. The results demonstrate the potential of the proposed framework to enable multi-agent collaboration in a tactical setting, where agents are limited in their computational and communication capabilities.

In the realm of vertical federated learning, a novel form of privacy breach has been identified, where an adversary with partial knowledge of a data participant's information can exploit the collaborative learning process to extract the full dataset. This paper delves into the theoretical underpinnings of this issue, examining how the learning algorithm can be manipulated to reveal private data, even when the attacker has limited access to the learning model. A practical demonstration of this vulnerability is provided, along with a proposed countermeasure that leverages differential privacy principles to safeguard sensitive data. The effectiveness of this approach is validated through comprehensive experiments.

Kernel density estimation is a widely used non-parametric method for estimating probability density functions. However, traditional kernel estimators often require a large amount of data and are computationally expensive, especially in high-dimensional settings. To address these limitations, we propose a novel kernel estimator based on pseudo-random Fourier attributes that is both computationally efficient and accurate. Our estimator is shown to be consistent under mild conditions and can be computed in O(d log d) time using the fast Fourier transform, where d represents the dimensionality of the data. We also demonstrate the effectiveness of our estimator through numerical experiments.

This research focuses on embedding a group G, which consists of symmetries for a regular n-dimensional polytope, into the product of regular polygons in n-dimensional space. By utilizing a recursive approach, we break down the regular n-dimensional polytope into regular (n-1)-dimensional polytopes and a regular 2-dimensional polygon, allowing us to embed G into the product of regular polygons in n-1 dimensional space and the product of regular polygons in 2-dimensional space. This process can be visualized through a tree-like structure, where each node represents a regular polytope and each edge represents a projection. We also introduce a method called Cartesian Decomposition, which splits the product of regular polygons in n-1 dimensional space into a product of regular (n-2)-dimensional polytopes, a product of regular 2-dimensional polygons, and a product of regular 3-dimensional polytopes. This method allows us to further decompose the embedding of G into the product of regular polygons in n-dimensional space into a product of regular (n-2)-dimensional polytopes, a product of regular 2-dimensional polygons, and a product of regular 3-dimensional polytopes.

Furthermore, it is shown that $\Sigma$ must be a round hypersphere in the $n+2$-dimensional sphere $\mathbb{S}^{n+2}$.

This research focuses on optimizing the allocation of wireless resources in a system where multiple users receive information and power from the same signal. The goal is to maximize the sum of data rates for users, subject to constraints on power transfer efficiency and signal quality. The problem is initially formulated for a single frequency band, and then extended to a multi-band scenario. The solution involves a two-step approach: first, determining the optimal power distribution across frequency bands, and second, allocating sub-channels to users. The results show that the problem can be solved efficiently, and the optimal allocation strategy can be found using a combination of convex optimization and integer programming techniques.

We developed a new method to analyze the growth of random Cayley graphs by introducing a novel sampling technique called avalanche sampling. This technique allows for the calculation of the probability distribution of the diameter of a random group generated by $d$ random elements and $r$ random relators. Our analysis reveals that the probability distribution of the diameter follows a power law with an exponent of $-2.00 \pm 0.01$ for small values of $r/d$, and a logarithmic decay for large values of $r/d$. Our findings are consistent with previous research on random groups and provide a more efficient way to sample random groups with a given diameter.

The detection of gravitational waves by interferometric detectors is hindered by the limited high-frequency response caused by the mirrors' suspension systems. This research proposes a novel design, the sloshing Sagnac interferometer, which can enhance the high-frequency response of detectors without increasing their overall optical power. This new design is based on a modified Sagnac interferometer and can be integrated into existing detectors with minimal changes. The research demonstrates that the sloshing Sagnac interferometer can significantly improve the high-frequency response of detectors, with a 10-fold increase in response at 1000 Hz and a 20-fold increase at 2000 Hz, without increasing the overall optical power. This design can be easily integrated into existing detectors with minimal changes.

In the context of multi-user multiple-input multiple-output (MU-MIMO) wireless networks, the stochastic access protocol (SAP) is a critical component that governs how devices contend for access to the shared medium. The performance of SAP is significantly influenced by the size of the control frame, which is used to exchange scheduling information. In this paper, we investigate the possibility of SAP devices transmitting their control frames simultaneously without interference, and we develop a novel analytical model to predict the non-intersecting visibility areas (NIVA) in SAP. Our model takes into account the spatial distribution of devices and the characteristics of the wireless channel, and we use it to study the impact of various SAP parameters on NIVA. Our findings reveal that NIVA is a valuable metric for evaluating the efficiency of SAP, and that the optimal SAP configuration can be determined by maximizing NIVA.

A novel type of three-body force, known as Big Apple, has been developed to address the issue of overbinding in neutron-rich nuclei. This force, which is density dependent and arises from the interaction of two nucleons with a meson field, is based on the $\sigma$ and $\omega$ mesons and is constructed to be consistent with the Big Apple di-baryon resonance. When applied to nuclear matter, the Big Apple force yields a saturation point with a saturation density of $0.16$ fm$^{-3}$ and a binding energy per nucleon of $-16$ MeV. Furthermore, calculations of finite nuclei using the Big Apple force demonstrate its ability to accurately predict the saturation point and reproduce the binding energies and radii of various nuclei. Additionally, the equation of state derived from these calculations predicts a neutron star radius of $11.5$ km for a $1.4$ solar mass neutron star, which is in agreement with recent observations.

In this study, we investigate the robustness of Molmer-Sorensen gates in trapped ion systems to frequency noise, which can arise from technical issues or fluctuations in the laser beam's focus. We find that balanced input intensities can significantly reduce the impact of frequency noise on gate fidelity, even when the noise is non-Gaussian and has a broad frequency spectrum. Our results are supported by numerical simulations and an analytical model, which demonstrate that balanced inputs can improve gate fidelity by up to 100 times compared to unequal input intensities. We also show that this approach can be used to create robust, high-fidelity gates in a variety of trapped ion systems, including those with multiple ions and different trap configurations.

We propose a new type of electronic structure in a crystal lattice, where a Dirac point exists and is protected by symmetry, with electrons behaving like fermions that follow the Pauli exclusion principle. This structure is characterized by a strong interaction between electrons, which is unusual for Dirac points in crystal lattices. We demonstrate that this strong interaction can be described using a simplified model, which can be used to calculate the properties of the material, including its conductivity and magnetic behavior. We also identify a new type of magnetic ordering that is protected by symmetry, which is unusual for materials with strong interactions. This new type of ordering is predicted to be stable at low temperatures and can be observed using experimental techniques such as neutron scattering. We also propose a specific crystal lattice that can be used to create this new type of electronic structure, which is unusual for materials with strong interactions. This specific crystal lattice is predicted to be stable and can be synthesized using standard techniques. We also predict that this material will exhibit unique properties such as high conductivity and unusual magnetic behavior, which can be observed using experimental techniques.

Theoretical predictions for the Standard Model are highly precise, and even the smallest discrepancies with experimental data can be significant. The search for new physics beyond the Standard Model is therefore a key focus of research. Theoretical models that predict the existence of a neutral lepton, which is massive and does not interact via the weak force, are particularly interesting. The NA62 experiment at CERN is well-suited to search for this type of particle through the study of $K^+ \to \pi^0 e^+ N$ decays. Theoretical predictions for the branching ratio of this decay are extremely small, but the NA62 experiment is capable of measuring branching ratios as small as $10^{-11}$, making it an ideal tool for this type of research. The authors of this paper present the expected sensitivity of the NA62 experiment to the neutral lepton, based on the number of $K^+$ decays that can be studied. They also provide a formula for the branching ratio of this decay in terms of the neutral lepton's mass and mixing angle, and discuss the expected sensitivity of the experiment to the mixing angle for different masses.

Neural language models excel at generating human-like text, but they often repeat phrases and lack diversity. This issue is particularly prevalent in models trained on vast amounts of data. We found that a simple neural model, based on $n$-gram language models, can effectively address this problem. By training a residual neural network to predict the difference between a basic $n$-gram model and a more advanced one, we achieved a significant reduction in perplexity. This approach also resulted in text that was more diverse and coherent, with less repetition. Our findings were validated through experiments on multiple datasets, including Wikipedia and Wikitext-2.

The task of 3D face alignment and reconstruction is challenging due to the variability in facial features and the impact of external factors such as pose, illumination, and occlusion. To address this issue, we propose a novel end-to-end framework called SADRNet, which is capable of performing accurate 3D face alignment and reconstruction from a single image. Our framework consists of two sub-networks that are self-aligned and share a common latent representation. The first sub-network, known as the appearance-driven network, is responsible for generating a rough estimate of the 3D face shape and texture. The second sub-network, called the geometry-driven network, is used to refine the rough estimate and produce the final 3D face shape and texture. The two sub-networks are self-supervised to ensure that they share a common latent representation, which is achieved through a self-alignment loss function. Our framework is designed to be robust to variations in pose, illumination, and occlusion, and it has been shown to outperform state-of-the-art methods on multiple benchmarks.

In this study, we examine the behavior of quantum fluctuations during the inflationary phase within the $\alpha$-attractor model, focusing on a specific parameter range where $\alpha$ is greater than 1000. We find that these fluctuations can lead to the formation of primordial black holes in the mass range of $10^{-3}$ to $10^{-1}$ solar masses. This finding is particularly significant as it could potentially explain the source of dark matter.

A labeled ordered tree with n nodes is a structure consisting of n nodes, each uniquely identified by a label from 1 to n, arranged in a specific order. In this paper, we investigate the concept of the deepest node in such a tree, defined as the node with the highest label among those at the greatest distance from the root. We derive the generating function for the number of labeled ordered trees with n nodes and a deepest node at a specific distance k from the root, and subsequently, the total count of labeled ordered trees with a deepest node label of d. Furthermore, we establish a bijection between labeled ordered trees with n nodes and a specific sequence of integers, and apply this bijection to obtain the generating function for the number of labeled ordered trees with n nodes and a deepest node label of d.

Election results are heavily influenced by the accuracy of vote tabulation systems.
Manual counting is prone to human error, while automated systems can be manipulated.
To address these issues, we propose iOCR, an informed optical symbol recognition
framework that leverages the inherent structure of ballot designs.
iOCR uses a pre-trained model to extract ballot features and then employs a
tabulation constraint to ensure the final results adhere to the expected format.
This approach is particularly effective for ballots with multiple choice options,
where the sum of votes for each option must equal the total number of ballots.
We evaluated iOCR on real-world ballot data from the 2020 US presidential election
in Los Angeles County, and found it to be highly accurate, with an average
tabulation error of less than 0.001% and a maximum error of 0.003%.
We also developed an open-source implementation of iOCR, which is available
at https://github.com/andrewjia/iOCR.

In the context of time series analysis, a linear model with a fixed number of lags is commonly used to forecast future values based on past data. However, this approach may not be suitable for non-stationary time series, as it assumes a constant relationship between past and present values. In this paper, we investigate the behavior of an over-parameterized linear model with a fixed number of lags when applied to non-stationary time series generated by an autoregressive process. We find that despite the model's inability to capture the underlying process, it can still accurately forecast future values due to the over-parameterization. This phenomenon, known as benign misfitting, is shown to occur under certain conditions and is demonstrated through both theoretical analysis and numerical simulations.

This paper introduces a cautious self-planning approach for storage operators in
distributed electricity markets. Unlike traditional methods, our approach takes into
account the uncertainty of future market prices and incorporates risk management
into the decision-making process. By using stochastic programming, we develop a
self-planning strategy that maximizes storage operators' profits while considering
potential risks. Our approach is demonstrated through numerical simulations,
showcasing its ability to balance risk and profit effectively.

Researchers have developed a computational model to simulate the atmospheric circulation of rocky planets with varying atmospheric compositions, gravity, and rotation rates. By analyzing the circulation patterns of these planets, the study found that the flow characteristics can be described using a combination of dimensionless numbers, including the Rossby number, Reynolds number, and radiative number. The study also divided the parameter space into four distinct regions, each with its own circulation pattern, and found that the boundaries between these regions are influenced by the planets' rotation rates, gravity, and atmospheric composition. The study provides a framework for understanding the atmospheric circulation of rocky planets and can be used to interpret observations of exoplanet atmospheres.

Deep neural networks are typically pre-trained on large datasets before being fine-tuned for specific tasks, a process that can be computationally expensive. A more efficient alternative involves training neural networks dynamically, where the network's weights are adjusted based on the characteristics of individual data points. This approach, known as data-driven learning, has been successfully applied in various scenarios, but its scalability to large-scale image classification tasks remains unexplored. In this study, we investigate the feasibility of dynamic learning on a massive dataset, the ImageNet, and develop a novel algorithm, the Dynamic Learning Algorithm (DLA), to facilitate this process. The DLA enables the network to be trained on individual images without the need for batch processing, a feature that is particularly beneficial for applications such as continual learning and edge computing. Experimental results demonstrate that the DLA achieves comparable performance to traditional batch processing methods, and that a network trained dynamically can effectively learn from a small set of labeled images in a subsequent task.

Researchers have developed a comprehensive CI simulation of exchange interactions between electrons in silicon, considering various valley states, and have incorporated multi-valley effective weight theory to reduce computational complexity. By utilizing this approach, the simulation can handle a wide range of donor configurations and impurity types without the need for additional calculations. The results obtained from this method are found to be consistent with previous findings and can serve as a reliable reference for calibrating more efficient approximations.

We investigated the transport properties of HgTe quantum trenches in the gapless phase, where electrons are confined in two dimensions within a narrow strip of the material. Our study focused on samples with widths ranging from 100 to 500 nanometers and lengths of up to 2 micrometers, and we measured their transport at extremely low temperatures, as low as 20 millikelvin. Our results showed that the mobility of electrons in these samples is limited by impurities, and that the mobility decreases as the width of the samples increases. We also found that the mobility is influenced by the orientation of the samples, and that the mobility is highest when the samples are oriented along the [100] crystallographic direction. Our findings are consistent with theoretical predictions, and they provide valuable insights into the transport properties of HgTe quantum trenches in the gapless phase.

In this paper, we address the challenge of dynamically allocating uplink and downlink time slots in TDD networks to maximize overall system throughput. We propose a novel approach that leverages a stochastic game model to predict user data rates and allocate time slots accordingly. Our method involves a two-step process: first, we use a machine learning algorithm to forecast user data rates, and then we apply a game-theoretic model to allocate time slots. Our results demonstrate that this approach can significantly improve overall system throughput compared to existing methods.

Our investigation reveals that Hamiltonian Neural Networks (HNNs) can effectively acquire gradients, enabling the application of gradient-based optimization techniques to refine their architecture. This discovery is particularly significant given the common practice of employing fixed activation functions in HNNs. Our research also highlights the potential for utilizing genetic algorithms to optimize HNNs' architecture, activation functions, and other components. To demonstrate this, we developed a novel genetic algorithm that optimizes HNNs' architecture and activation functions, resulting in improved performance on the Atari suite of games.

The rapid advancement of machine learning has led to the development of complex systems that are increasingly difficult for humans to understand and control. This lack of transparency and explainability poses a significant challenge, particularly in critical applications where human oversight is essential. To address this issue, we propose a novel framework for a human-in-the-loop multi-agent system that enables a human to actively participate in the training process of a machine learning model. In this framework, a human user provides feedback on the reliability of the model's predictions and can provide additional data to enhance the model's training. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through a proof-of-concept implementation, showing that it can significantly improve the model's performance and provide a more transparent and controllable machine learning system.

We define a quantum invariant for chains within the three-dimensional torus times an interval, denoted as $T^2 \times I$, and establish that this invariant satisfies the property of invariance under isotopy and the Stern-Berger relation. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this quantum invariant, when applied to a specific chain, yields a value that is proportional to the volume of the chain, thus exhibiting a behavior akin to the volume conjecture.

Word sense disambiguation (WSD) is a challenging task that involves determining the correct meaning of ambiguous words within a specific context. This research introduces a novel approach called Context-Gloss Enhancement (CGE), which leverages the definitions of ambiguous words to improve the accuracy of WSD. CGE creates a new training set by combining the definitions of ambiguous words with their corresponding context, which is then used to train a neural network-based WSD model. The results of this study demonstrate that CGE outperforms the baseline method in both the Senseval-3 and SemEval-2013-WSD tasks.

The reciprocal Gamma function can be expressed as an integral in the form:
$1/\Gamma(z) = \int_0^\infty e^{-t} f(t,z) dt$.
This paper derives a series of integral representations for the reciprocal Gamma function by utilizing the substitution $t = \ln x$ in the standard definition of the Gamma function.
The resulting integrals are shown to be equivalent to previously established integral representations, including those by Wrench, Stieltjes, and Nörlund.
The paper also derives a new integral representation for the reciprocal Gamma function.

A novel approach is proposed to identify top quark production in proton-nucleus collisions, utilizing the distinctive decay signature of top quarks into a lepton and a neutrino. This method leverages the presence of a high transverse momentum photon from the fragmentation of a gluino or top quark, which can be detected in forward calorimeters. By combining this photon with a lepton from top quark decay, a unique signature emerges that can be used to pinpoint top quark production. A detailed analysis of the background and signal efficiency is conducted, and the optimal search region is identified. The study reveals that top quark production can be detected in proton-lead collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 8.16 TeV with a cross-section of 0.1 picobarns, and in proton-oxygen collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 200 TeV with a cross-section of 0.1 picobarns.

End-to-end text-to-SQL parsing converts natural language queries into structured SQL representations, which are then used to retrieve data from databases. This process is crucial for enabling users to access information from complex databases without needing technical knowledge. However, existing parsers often produce inaccurate results when dealing with unfamiliar domains, which can lead to incorrect data retrieval. To address this issue, we propose a novel cross-domain parser that leverages a support task to facilitate knowledge transfer between different domains. Our parser is designed to be modular and can be easily adapted to new domains with minimal effort.
